verified_claims: Lemma 1.1: every pair of terms has gcd > 1 (direct from the defining minimality), all terms lie in S_infinity, and any x in S_infinity with x >= a_1 that is not a term would fit between consecutive terms a_n < x < a_{n+1} (strictly increasing integer sequence is unbounded) and beat a_{n+1} in minimality — so the sequence is exactly the increasing enumeration of S_infinity ∩ [a_1, ∞).
Lemma 1.2 (killing property): if x > a_1 and x ∉ S_infinity, some earlier term a_i < x is coprime to x; verified via the same inter-term placement and minimality argument.
S_infinity is closed under multiples; every element has a divisor minimal in S_infinity (finite divisor set), giving S_infinity = ∪_{h∈M} h·Z_{>0}; M is nonempty since a_1 ∈ S_infinity.

Lemma 2.1: with M = {h_1,…,h_k} and L = lcm, membership in S_infinity is L-periodic for all positive integers (h_i | m ⟺ h_i | m+L); the blocks [a_1+jL, a_1+(j+1)L) each contain exactly the translates b_r+jL, so a_{jT+r} = b_r+jL and a_{n+T} = a_n + L for all n ≥ 1.
Every h ∈ M is squarefree (h/p has the same support, hence stays in S_infinity), so h = π(supp h).

C is exactly the family of inclusion-minimal transversals of {supp(a_i)}; verified both directions (proper subset of a minimal generator's support gives a strictly smaller squarefree divisor in S_infinity, and conversely a divisor of π(t) in S_infinity has support a transversal). C is an antichain.
Lemma 3.1: each supp(a_i) contains a member of C.
Lemma 3.2: members of C pairwise intersect — π(c)^k ≥ a_1 is a term by Lemma 1.1 with support exactly c, and every d ∈ C transverses all term supports.
Lemma 3.3: any finite set of primes Q meeting all of C meets every supp(a_i) (by 3.1), so π(Q) ∈ S_infinity and the squarefree minimal divisor h | π(Q) yields c = supp(h) ∈ C with c ⊆ Q.

Lemma 4.1 (descent): if π(d) > a_1·p then F = d∖{p} is not a transversal (minimality of d), so π(F) ∉ S_infinity and π(F) > a_1; Lemma 1.2 gives a term a_i < π(F) coprime to π(F); the h ∈ M dividing a_i has e = supp(h) ∈ C with e ∩ F = ∅, π(e) ≤ a_i < π(F) = π(d)/p, and e ∩ d ≠ ∅ (Lemma 3.2) forces p ∈ e; so π strictly decreases while preserving p ∈ d, terminating at π(d) ≤ a_1·p.

Section 5: if C were infinite, U = ∪C is infinite (else C ⊆ finite powerset); distinct p_j ∈ U give d_j ∋ p_j with π(d_j) ≤ a_1·p_j, so π(Q_j) ≤ a_1 with Q_j = d_j∖{p_j}; pigeonhole over the finitely many squarefree integers ≤ a_1 gives an infinite subfamily with Q_j = Q and p_j ∉ Q distinct; for each e ∈ C choosing j with p_j ∉ e and using Lemma 3.2 shows e ∩ Q ≠ ∅, so Q is a finite transversal of C; Lemma 3.3 then gives c ∈ C with c ⊆ Q ⊊ d_j, contradicting the antichain property. Hence C and M are finite.

Degenerate cases handled: M and C are nonempty (a_1 ∈ S_infinity), Q = ∅ cannot be a transversal since members of C are nonempty, candidate integers for a_{n+1} always exist (e.g. a_1⋯a_n), and T ≥ 1 since a_1 ∈ S_infinity.

Overall composition: Lemmas 1.1–1.2 → structure of M/C (Sections 2–3) → descent (4.1) → finiteness (Section 5) → Lemma 2.1 yields T, L with a_{n+T} = a_n + L for every n; no circularity (finiteness is never assumed in the lemmas used to prove it).
Sanity checks on concrete instances (a_1 = 2, 3, 4, 15, 25) confirm S_infinity = multiples of a fixed integer and quasi-linearity, consistent with the theorem and Lemma 2.1.
summary: The proof is correct, complete, and self-contained. It characterizes the sequence as the increasing enumeration of the divisibility-upward-closed set S_infinity, shows that if the set M of minimal generators is finite then membership is periodic with period lcm(M), immediately yielding a_{n+T} = a_n + L, and then proves M finite by identifying it with squarefree minimal transversals C of the term-support hypergraph and deriving a contradiction from infinitude via the descent bound π(d) ≤ a_1·p (Lemma 4.1), a pigeonhole on squarefree integers ≤ a_1, the pairwise-intersection property (Lemma 3.2), the transversal-lifting property (Lemma 3.3), and the antichain property. All quantifier steps, the descent termination, degenerate cases (empty Q, nonemptiness of C, unboundedness of the sequence, existence of candidates), and the periodic block enumeration were independently re-derived and check out.
transfer_assessment: Reusable: representing a greedy sequence as the increasing enumeration of a membership set (Lemma 1.1) plus a 'killing' contrapositive (Lemma 1.2) obtained purely from minimality of the greedy choice.

Reusable: divisibility-upward-closed sets of integers are finite unions of arithmetic progressions once their minimal generators are finite; period = lcm of generators, and density counting gives the (T, L) quasi-linearity. Applies to any eventually-periodic membership function.
Reusable: translating divisibility questions into a hypergraph of prime supports; minimal generators ↔ inclusion-minimal transversals; antichain + pairwise-intersection structure.

Reusable: descent arguments on the multiplicative weight π(·) with a threshold bound (here π(d) ≤ a_1·p), combined with pigeonhole over squarefree integers below a fixed bound to force infinitely many sets sharing a common core — a standard route to finiteness of antichain families.
Reusable: the trick of taking a large power π(c)^k ≥ a_1 to make a prescribed prime-support occur as an actual term of the sequence.

Misleading if transferred carelessly: pairwise intersection of minimal transversals (Lemma 3.2) is special to this gcd structure (powers of a member are terms) and fails for general hypergraphs; similarly, Lemma 3.3's 'every finite transversal of C contains a member of C' relies on the specific generator structure, not general transversal theory. Also, periodicity holds from n = 1 (not merely eventually) only because Lemma 1.1 is global, not asymptotic.
